faq.question: Does a blank in the freeze-drying column mean I can sell freeze-dried food in that state?
faq.answer: No. It records that the agency's published material does not use the term. What that silence means depends on the architecture of the state's law: in a state whose rule enumerates a closed list of allowed products, an unnamed product sits outside the list [52][53]; in a state that defines the boundary by food characteristic, such as Tennessee's non-TCS category [61] or Minnesota's pH-and-water-activity test [37], an unnamed process is not thereby excluded.

faq.question: Which jurisdictions name freeze-drying explicitly?
faq.answer: Twenty-three of the 51 rows in the table: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, Missouri, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah and West Virginia. They do not agree: California lists a freeze-dried category [10], New York prohibits freeze-dried foods [49], New Jersey prohibits the machines themselves [46], and Oregon allows the process for confectionery only [56].

faq.question: Is there a federal cottage food law?
faq.answer: No. Each state carves the exemption out of its own food establishment licensing law, and in several states a county or local health department registers or inspects on top of the state rule. Federal regulation sits behind rather than above it: the acidified-foods rule defines its scope using water activity above 0.85 with a finished equilibrium pH of 4.6 or below [1], and multistate extension guidance places frozen and dehydrated food operations under federal current good manufacturing practice [3].

faq.question: Which states publish an actual number for water activity?
faq.answer: Arizona publishes both thresholds for lab verification, water activity below 0.85 and pH at or below 4.6 [6]. Minnesota states the same pair as the non-potentially-hazardous test [37]. Illinois states the water activity figure advisorily: \u201caim for a water activity of 0.85 or less\u201d; it also requires a lab pH test for acidified and fermented products [24]. North Carolina [50] and the District of Columbia [16] publish a testing route rather than a threshold.

faq.question: How current is this directory?
faq.answer: Every row was checked on 2026-09-06 against the linked document, and the next scheduled check is 2026-12-06. Several linked pages were revised during 2025 and 2026, and a few state programs in the table have pending or recently amended statutes, West Virginia's new cottage foods article among them [68]. Check the linked page before relying on any row.

bodyHtml:
The short version: this page is a directory of the agency that administers cottage food law in each of the 51 US jurisdictions, with a link and a note on whether that agency's published text names freeze-drying at all. Of the 51 rows below, 23 name freeze-drying explicitly and 28 do not. The ones that do name it disagree in both directions, with California listing a category titled “Dried, Dehydrated, and Freeze-Dried Foods” [10] while New York puts “Freeze-dried foods” on its prohibited list [49]. Everything here describes what an agency publishes; it does not tell you what you may sell.

What this is, and what it is not

This is a directory, not advice. Each row names the agency, links its published page, and records one narrow fact: whether the words “freeze-dried,” “freeze dried” or “freeze drying” appear in the material that agency publishes. Nothing in the table says a product is legal or illegal where you live. Cottage food rules change by statute, by administrative rule and by agency page revision, and several of the pages linked below were revised during the year they were checked.

Two structural facts make the table readable. First, there is no federal cottage food statute; each state carves an exemption out of its own food establishment licensing law, and in several states a county or local health department administers or inspects on top of it. The federal layer that does exist sits behind the state rules: the acidified-foods regulation, for instance, defines its own scope using a water activity “greater than 0.85” together with a finished equilibrium pH of 4.6 or below [1], and multistate extension guidance places frozen and dehydrated food operations under federal current good manufacturing practice [3]. Second, the load-bearing idea in every state list is the non-TCS concept. Penn State Extension states the pairing plainly: TCS foods have “high moisture (aw > 0.85) and/or low acid content (pH > 4.6)” [2]. Dried and freeze-dried products reach non-TCS status by moisture removal, and most cottage food statutes never defined a test for it.

Cottage food authority by jurisdiction

Alphabetical. A “No” in the last column is a recorded silence in the material that was checked; it is not permission and it is not prohibition.

Every row was checked on the same date against the linked document.

Why silence means opposite things in opposite states

The 28 silent rows are not one finding. They sit inside two different statutory architectures, and the same blank means the reverse thing in each.

  • Enumerated-permitted-list states publish a closed list of allowed products. Ohio is the clearest case: the allowed set is fixed by administrative rule, and every dried entry either presupposes a commercially dried ingredient or is a blend of dry ingredients [52][53]. In that architecture, a product absent from the list is outside the list.
  • Exclusionary and food-freedom states permit what is not excluded, and define the boundary by food characteristic rather than by process. Tennessee's operative category is non-TCS homemade food [61]; Minnesota states the test as pH 4.6 or below, or water activity 0.85 or less [37]. In that architecture, an unnamed process is not thereby excluded.

This is why no single yes/no column is safe to act on by itself, and why the column above records the presence of language rather than a legal conclusion.

Where a state publishes a number, not a category

A small number of jurisdictions resolve the moisture question with a measurement instead of a product list. These are the ones that publish a threshold or a testing route in their cottage food material.

JurisdictionWhat is published
ArizonaNumeric thresholds for establishing shelf stability by lab testing: “Water Activity Testing: results must fall below 0.85 aw” and “pH Testing: results must test acidic at 4.6 pH or below” [6]
North Carolina“Inspectors may require that your product be tested for pH and/or water activity prior to the inspection”; laboratories supply a Process Authority Letter, required for acidified foods [50]
District of ColumbiaFor foods not on the approved list, applicants submit confirmation of pH value and water activity from a state-accredited laboratory [16]
IllinoisAdvisory rather than documentary on moisture: “For safety, aim for a water activity of 0.85 or less” — while a lab pH test is required for acidified and fermented products [24]
New JerseyResolves it categorically instead of numerically, with the stated reason that “The process of freeze-drying or dehydrating fruits using a machine cannot reliably lower the moisture content to a safe level” [46]
MinnesotaStates the non-potentially-hazardous test itself: pH 4.6 or below, or water activity 0.85 or less [37]

One further pattern is worth naming because it changes which page a reader should trust. In Oklahoma, freeze-drying is named by the extension service [55] and not by the agency bulletin [54]. In Colorado, it appears on the agency page [11] in both directions at once. Where agency text and extension text differ, the agency text is the one that governs the program, and it is the one linked in the table above. If your answer matters, the durable move is to put the question to your own state agency in writing and keep the reply alongside your records.

What we could not source

  • Florida's live program page. The FDACS cottage food page returned 403 at the network egress layer and is disallowed by robots. The Florida row rests on FDACS guidance document FDACS-P-02072 as hosted by extension [17]. Whether the live page carries dried or freeze-dried language absent from the guidance is open, not closed.
  • Washington's WSDA cottage food page body. Not retrievable this pass; the Washington row rests on the statute and rule text instead [66][67].
  • Ohio's ODA program page URL. Not resolved; the row uses the administrative rule [52] and the agency fact sheet [53].
  • Virginia's VDACS HTML landing page. Not retrieved; the row uses the VDACS FAQ PDF [65].
  • Utah Administrative Code R70-560 rule text. The published URL now returns only a redirect notice, so the rule's own text, as distinct from the UDAF page and application form [63], was not read.
  • Wyoming's Food Freedom Act Q&A. The agency page exposes it as a download link only [70]; it is the single most likely Wyoming location for a freeze-drying statement and it was not retrieved.
  • North Dakota's post-2021 administrative rules. The chapter that would carry an allowed-foods list is largely repealed and no replacement was located; the row rests on the statute [51].
  • Vermont's Act 42 (2025) codified text. The general licensing section contains no cottage food definition or cap; the Vermont row rests on the Department of Health page alone [64].
  • South Carolina's current agency name. The Clemson guidance retains the pre-reorganization agency name [59]; no successor state agency page was fetched to confirm who administers the law today.
  • The District's approved-foods list. Neither DC Health document publishes an affirmative allowed list: only prohibitions plus the laboratory submission pathway [15][16].
  • West Virginia's Article 40 status. The 2026 committee amendment creating a new cottage foods article was located, but whether it was enacted, and its effective date, were not confirmed; the row rests on the agency page [68].
  • Kansas's statutory citation. No statute number appears on the located Kansas Department of Agriculture pages; the state publishes an exemption list rather than a cottage food registration [29].
  • Louisiana's agency program page. None located. The Louisiana row rests on the statute [32].
  • Any ranking. No agency in the set publishes a comparative ordering of jurisdictions by permissiveness, and the columns are not commensurable: North Carolina has no revenue cap but requires inspection [50]; Michigan has a cap but no inspection [36]; Arizona has neither cap nor fee but requires continuously maintained food handler training [6]. No ordering is offered here.
  • Sublime Pantry has bench-tested nothing in this article. Every entry above is a reading of somebody else's published page on a stated date.

Next

  • The economics of selling what you dry covers what the rules cost once you price a unit.
  • What water activity measures is the threshold several of these statutes are written around.
  • What freeze-drying does to candy, a category that comes up repeatedly in the rows above.
